Shaken and Stirred by the Search for the Next James Bond

The question may be less who will inherit the mantle than who in his right mind would want to.

By Anthony Lane

How was your weekend? Did you find an unexpected person in your bed? Did you slay a couple of heavies with your bare hands, then do it again, with extra venom? Did you save the world? If not, I have bad news: you are not the next James Bond. The quest for a new occupant of what remains, despite everything, the hottest seat in cinema—the role of 007—reached its latest climax on October 23rd to 25th, in London. Thither, “according to several sources,” in the words of The Hollywood Reporter, a chosen few were summoned to butch it out for the ultimate honor. Talk about a Bonding exercise.

Who those sources were cannot, of course, be revealed. Like purveyors of royal gossip, Bond whisperers never identify themselves; to do so would be to court the fate of Professor Dent, in “Dr. No,” who is shot after attempting—the fool!—to kill Bond with a mere tarantula. (The actor playing Dent, Anthony Dawson, had already tried to do away with Grace Kelly, in “Dial M for Murder,” and been stabbed for his pains. How epic can fails be?) Anyway, we are now informed, reliably or not, that the final contestants for the part of 007 include Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, and Josh O’Connor. Otherwise known, as any TV addict will tell you, as that guy from “Slow Horses,” that guy from “Masters of the Air,” and that guy with the ears who played Prince Charles in “The Crown.” Also allegedly in the running: Jack O’Connell, who, in “Sinners,” became one of the first vampires to dance an Irish jig. In a solemn aside, the Reporter adds, “It is unclear who else may be testing.”

In short, we haven’t a clue. In recent years, all too many names have drifted in and out of the frame: Idris Elba, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Henry Cavill, Jacob Elordi, Richard Madden, Tom Hardy, Theo James, and Paul Mescal, although, given how miserable Mescal looked when he had to fight someone who was riding a rhino, in “Gladiator 2,” his odds may have lengthened. Age is another disqualifier. Elba, now fifty-four, was touted as a possible Bond for so long that his chance has come and gone, whereas Lowden, Turner, and O’Connor are thirty-six. A decade ago, the Irish actor Aidan Turner (you may have seen him in “Poldark,” on PBS) was all the rage, and his compound of intensity and levity, like that of his countryman Pierce Brosnan, appeared to fit the bill—one of Bond’s defining knacks, after all, is for orchestrating the victory of good over evil without taking either of them too seriously. But Aidan Turner is forty-three, and, like most of us, he will surely recall the crowning exchange, between hero and villain, that lends “The Spy Who Loved Me” its philosophical weight:

“Your time is running out, Stromberg.”

“Yours, too, Mr. Bond. Yours, too. And faster than you think.”

One man whose mortal time ran out this year, to the understandable dismay of his admirers, was Sam Neill. Born in Northern Ireland, he grew up in New Zealand before relocating to Australia, and that cultural backdrop, fronted by his other virtues, might have made him an excellent Bond. He was dashing, effortlessly amused, and quite unassuming in his command of our attention—so much so, indeed, that he specified how badly he did not wish to play 007. “I wouldn’t have been any good and I wouldn’t have enjoyed it,” he once said. In 1986, nonetheless, he went to Pinewood Studios, outside London, for a screen test. It survives online, enabling lunatics like me, who treasure films that never came to pass, to watch Neill intone the sacred liturgy of Bond. Entering his bedroom, he discovers that he is not alone:

“So, you’re Tatiana Romanova.”

“My friends call me Tania.”

“My friends call me Bond. James Bond.”

There is almost too much to unpack here. First, the intruder, lying in wait and in bed, is gamely played for the purposes of the audition by Fiona Fullerton, who only the year before had been in “A View to a Kill,” Roger Moore’s last movie as Bond. Second, where is the choker? The sequence is lifted from the second Bond film, “From Russia with Love,” in which, as Tatiana, Daniela Bianchi—lest we forget, a former Miss Universo Italia—wears a black choker and barely anything else. Details matter, as they did for Ian Fleming, who, in the original novel of “From Russia with Love,” not only bedecks Tatiana with “a quarter-inch black velvet ribbon round her neck” but also saddles her with an awkward, if well-meaning, gaffe:

“You are very handsome,” she said. She searched for a comparison that would give him pleasure. “You are like an American film star.”

She was startled by his reaction. “For God’s sake! That’s the worst insult you can pay a man!”

One wonders if this repartee, which was wisely omitted from the script, rang in the ears of James Brolin, who reënacted the same scene, with a British accent and a touch of aplomb, for his screen test, in 1982. He was up for the role of Bond in “Octopussy,” and his Tatiana, for the test, was played by Maud Adams. (No Bondian needs reminding that she had earned her spurs as Scaramanga’s doomed girlfriend in “The Man with the Golden Gun.” Do keep up.) In the event, although Brolin believed that the part was his, and even had orders to “prepare certain muscles for certain things I wasn’t adept at yet,” Moore returned for his sixth excursion as Bond in “Octopussy,” opposite Adams. The state of Moore’s muscles is unrecorded.

There is another snippet of Bond that has been used to challenge contenders for the throne. It comes from “GoldenEye,” and it consists of Bond introducing himself to Xenia Onatopp, one of his nemeses, and smirking maturely as he hears her name. In 2005, with “Casino Royale” on the cards, actors such as Sam Worthington, Antony Starr, Rupert Friend, and Henry Cavill (then a stripling of twenty-two) were invited to pronounce the words “Bond—James Bond” for the camera. Casual clips display their halting efforts. Eventually, all the young dudes lost out to Daniel Craig, who, in the course of five films, went on to make the role his own—and, it must be said, to demonstrate the toll that it took. Craig’s appeal was undimmed to the end, yet the joy slowly faded from his gaze, and maybe the question we ought to be asking is not “Who will be the next Bond?” but “Who in his right mind would want to be Bond?” Also, “Why do we still care who Bond is or isn’t?” Oh, and one last complicating factor: Bond is dead.

“Appeasement, Ohio”

By George Saunders

Yeow, the old Ohio place. My cousin Maribeth looks about the same. Her son Kip’s a man now: big boy, around two-fifty, thick pink arms like tattooed hams.

I meet Carl, Maribeth’s third, possibly fourth, husband: nice guy, sprig of hair on the front of his head like a Kewpie, but white hair, not blond.

Also Mick, a pal of Kip’s.

“Eggs?” Carl says.

“No, thanks,” I say.

“I will,” Kip says.

“Scrambled,” Mick says.

“Unless you boys no longer believe in eggs,” Carl says. “Or chickens. Mick, still believe in chickens?”

“Yes, sir, still believe in chickens,” Mick says, maintaining discipline.

“Upstairs, in the attic?” Carl says. “Kip? A box of Civil War coat buttons, from your great-great-whoever. Plus his bayonet.”

“Anyone can make a button,” Mick says.

“Anyone can put a bayonet in an attic,” Kip says.

“Look how I trained him up,” Mick says.

I’m trying to connect the beaming giant that is Kip with the shy little guy I used to carry up to bed.

Carl sets down a plate of toast.

“Food for the brain trust,” he says.

“You’re being sarcastic,” says Mick.

“Ma’s a believer,” says Kip.

“Well, you kids make a strong case,” Maribeth says.

“For example,” says Kip, spinning his Dell around.

Headline: “Gettysburg Archaeology Proves No Battle.” Author: “Ned.” Photo: metal detector leaning against a palm tree. Nailed to the tree, a laminated sign: “Locale: Gettysburg, PA.”

“Zero palm trees in Pennsylvania,” Carl says.

“That you know of,” Kip says.

“That anyone knows of,” Carl says.

“What’s your source?” Mick says in a faux-military voice.

“Having been there many times,” Carl says.

“Have you walked literally every square foot of the state?” Mick says.

“Shit’s sake,” Carl says.

“Language,” Maribeth says. “We don’t swear in this house.”

Blair Metcalf is the principal UX engineer at Reddit and the creator of Reddit Proto, an internal platform that helps designers and product managers build production-like prototypes without touching GitHub. In this episode, he shows how the system combines real Reddit data, reusable scaffolds, Cursor annotations, and a custom design system MCP to turn ideas into shareable prototypes. Biggest takeaways:

  1. The best prototyping tools hide complexity without limiting capability. Reddit’s desktop app handles repositories, branches, and scaffolding behind the scenes, so designers never touch Git. What remains is a simple path from idea to production-shaped prototype.

  2. Mock data makes prototypes less convincing. Reddit lets people sign in to prototypes with their real accounts, filling feeds, searches, and communities with familiar content. Leadership can evaluate the actual experience instead of mentally correcting for placeholders.

  3. Annotations become powerful when they include code context. Reddit’s harness attaches each comment to the relevant component, design-system guidance, and the user’s intent before sending it to Cursor. That context turns a short annotation into a accurate working edit instead of a guess.

  4. A custom design-system MCP is what turns AI into a reliable builder. Blair’s team mapped Reddit’s tokens, components, and workflows directly to production code. Cursor therefore knows which component to use, how it should look, and where the code belongs.

  5. The feature capsule makes design handoffs traceable instead of lossy. A designer submits a Figma link, and the system maps each element to production components, incorporates previous engineering feedback, and generates a structured PRD with acceptance criteria. The result is a handoff with far less room for interpretation.

  6. The best AI prototypers are not necessarily the most technical. Reddit’s standout users include a visual designer and an animator with no engineering background. Their advantage is strong product context, a clear vision, and a willingness to experiment without worrying about breaking things.

  7. At 700 prototypes, discovery becomes as important as creation. Reddit is building a searchable console with tags, team filters, and platform filters so employees can find related experiments. Keeping prototypes public internally creates visibility that scattered Figma folders never could.

  8. Real components and real data create instant alignment. When leaders can open a shareable prototype built with Reddit’s design system and their own account data, implementation questions stop dominating the review. The biggest speed gain comes from removing the uncertainty that once delayed decisions.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. Claude Duet is the most polished personal agent launch yet. From onboarding onward, it clearly explains what it can do, what it can access, and how to begin. Claire found even the early TestFlight builds trustworthy and roughly a hundred times more polished than OpenAI’s Dots at launch.

  2. Duet is built around thoughtful agent primitives. It inherits Claude plugins and connectors, tracks what the user and the agent are each working on, and brings existing artifacts into the experience. Slack-like channels also keep focused work, such as sales, separate from the main conversation.

  3. Duet is designed for the middle of the market. Anthropic is targeting entrepreneurs, small-business owners, PMs, and executives, rather than casual consumers or power users managing dozens of agents. It feels like a proactive, mobile companion to Cowork.

  4. A proactive agent has to give people a reason to return. After onboarding and a few tasks, Duet stopped nudging Claire. Its quiet notifications are elegant, but a short morning briefing is not enough to keep an easily forgotten agent in someone’s daily routine.

  5. Latency is a product problem, not merely a model problem. Opus 5.5 produced solid work, but parallel tasks routinely took more than 10 minutes with little visible feedback. Claire’s experience suggests that a faster agent with slightly weaker output may feel more useful than a smarter one that disappears while working.

Sales pipeline analysis worked quickly through existing connectors, while inbox and Slack triage missed some priorities and important context. A sales deck was decent but off-brand, and ticket shopping worked without fully closing the loop.

Even a five-person business needs agents that can operate collaboratively rather than remaining single-player mobile experiences.

  9. Duet is worth trying, but it has not earned a permanent place in Claire’s stack. The design, models, connectors, and artifact support create a strong foundation. To win the personal-agent race, it still needs to become faster, more proactive, available on desktop, and shareable with a team.

In November 2025, Sally Rooney submitted a witness statement to Britain’s High Court, on behalf of a co-founder of Palestine Action, Huda Ammori. The court was considering the UK government’s decision to designate Palestine Action as a terrorist group. Ammori was arguing that this constituted an authoritarian ban on protest. In support, Rooney said that her books might have to be withdrawn from sale in Britain, and that, "The disappearance of my work from bookshops would mark a truly extreme incursion by the state into the realm of artistic expression."

Almost a year later, this has come to pass. Rooney’s publisher, Faber, has taken her books off sale, with her consent, because they fear a prosecution. The Terrorism Act of 2000 makes it illegal to provide money to anyone where you have reasonable cause to suspect it might be used for the purposes of terrorism. After the 2025 ban on Palestine Action (PA), Rooney said, repeatedly, that she continues to support it, “in whatever way I can”. That constitutes a pretty firm basis for suspicion. It is also illegal to express support for a banned organisation. Rooney has made her statements of support from Ireland, where she lives. Had she made them here, she might have faced prosecution. Thousands of people in Britain have been arrested for holding signs which say, “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action”.

To be clear, the British government hasn’t banned Rooney’s books. It isn’t illegal to sell or distribute them; you can easily pick them up second-hand. Faber’s withdrawal is voluntary. Faber could, in theory, have kept the books on sale and withheld the payments, but decided that wouldn’t be fair on their author. They were under no pressure from the government to stop paying Rooney and in truth it seems unlikely that the Crown Prosecution Service would have picked this fight. But it’s a reasonable precaution for them to take.1

There is, of course, a political motivation for the withdrawal, at least on Rooney’s behalf. She wants to highlight the negative effects of the ban on PA. In this, she has been very successful. Millions of Sally Rooney readers have been shocked by this turn of events and many will blame the government. To anyone of common sense, it seems absurd that novels about the love lives of Irish millennials should be made unavailable on the basis of terrorism law. It also seems crazy that middle-class pensioners holding placards should be treated as engaging in terrorist activity. Even those who aren’t fans of Rooney’s books, or her politics, may feel sympathetic to her cause.

But what is her cause, exactly? What is actually at stake here, beyond the banning of one particular organisation?

The literary world is in no doubt: it has enthusiastically adopted Rooney’s framing of the issue, as set out in her statement to the High Court. The New Statesman has gathered an impressive list of writers and intellectuals, and Gary Lineker, to sign an open letter to the government. This is its admirably short text:

Sally Rooney is a writer, not a terrorist. Her books must be available to the public. Their withdrawal from sale, on the basis of ill-conceived and draconian anti-terror legislation, is an affront to basic principles of free speech and expression so long taken for granted in this country. We categorically reject censorship – whether direct or indirect – and urge the government to change course, amending the legislation which has led us to this point of repressive absurdity.

The letter comes attached to an op-ed by Tanjil Rashid, editor of the New Statesman’s (superb) culture pages. It opens by invoking the name of Salman Rushdie, before going on to develop the comparison:

The last time books by a controversial author were withdrawn from retailers was during the more heated affair over The Satanic Verses. The UK government, of course, had not banned Salman Rushdie’s novel, but a climate of fear had led to its voluntary withdrawal. The government has not intentionally banned Rooney’s books either; the withdrawal of her work is equally voluntary, but based, likewise, on a climate of fear. The difference lies in how the fear has been stoked. Rushdie’s censor was terrorism – actual terrorists, who spilled real blood over his book. In Rooney’s case, it is legislation.

Now, I like (and subscribe to) the New Statesman, but I don’t like this comparison. I find it crass, even obscene, caveat and all. But we’ll get back to Rushdie. Before we do so, let’s look at the question of whether the Rooney case is really about what she and her fellow writers say it’s about.

Share

Is it about freedom of artistic expression? Usually, when people invoke the spectre of censorship it’s because a work of art has been banned, or an artist has been punished for self-expression. But one thing all parties agree on here is that there is little politically subversive about Normal People or Intermezzo. That these books have been removed from the shelves has nothing to do with the words inside them. Nobody in government has ever sought to ban them. Their disappearance may be a secondary effect of a restriction of speech but it is not because the artist concerned, or anyone else, has had their artistic expression curbed.

Is it about the right to dissent? The New Statesman thinks so:

Rooney has shown us that the laws aren’t fit for purpose, that writers cannot always dissent from government policy with the outspokenness and commitment that is their right.

But this doesn’t seem right, either. Writers dissent vehemently from government policy on Israel every day. Insofar as Rooney has put her publisher in legal jeopardy, it is not because she has criticised the government, and in fact it is grossly misleading to imply that it is. It is because she has said, or implied, that she will give the money that she receives from the publisher to a designated terrorist organisation. That’s it. The fact that Rooney is an author is irrelevant to the legal situation. Let’s imagine she is not a writer but a businesswoman, the owner of a vegan granola brand which exports to the UK. If she happened to tell a local paper that she might use the proceeds from these sales to support Palestine Action, Waitrose would now be in the same position as Faber.

In truth this case has nothing to do with the suppression of radical art, or subversive ideas, or dissent. It’s about an illegal flow of money. For the writers and artists who signed the New Statesman letter, that might be a disappointingly prosaic way to put it, but it’s accurate.

Nonetheless, we shouldn’t dismiss the free speech question entirely. Funding aside, any expression of support for Palestine Action would expose Rooney to prosecution, if she were in Britain. Those peaceful, placard-holding protestors who spent the night in a police cell can testify to that. That does seem like an objectionable curb on speech and protest, even if it’s not specifically to do with arts and letters. But I think we should be clear, once more, about what we’re objecting to.

The New Statesman’s open letter blames the withdrawal of Rooney’s books on “draconian anti-terror legislation”. Nowhere in the letter or editorial do we learn what specific law they are objecting to, or what change they would propose. We are forced to guess. Are they objecting to the proscription of terrorist organisations in general? I doubt it. Everyone seems to agree that organisations like Al-Qaeda should be banned. Are they objecting to a law which bans people from providing funds to individuals if they suspect it will end up with terrorists? I hope not - that seems pretty sensible to me.

Perhaps their objection is to the criminalisation of any expression of support for a terrorist organisation? They would be on stronger ground here. If you’re a free speech advocate, you might well argue that it should be legal to cheer on a terrorist group, even if doing so is clearly abhorrent. But somehow, I doubt this is what those writers want. The signatories of that letter should ask themselves if they would be happy with the government making it legal to speak up for, or hold placards on behalf of, a neo-Nazi group like Sonnenkrieg Division, also banned under this law. Looking at the list of names, I’d be very surprised if so. I don’t think they are objecting to legislation at all. I think they are objecting to the proscription of Palestine Action under this legislation.

Now, this more tightly defined dispute might be worth taking up cudgels for. But before taking a closer look at whether PA should be proscribed, let’s mark how far we’ve travelled. We started by asking whether this is really about artistic self-expression, as Rooney and her fellow writers claim. It doesn’t seem to be. Then we asked whether it’s about free speech and the right to dissent. Not much going on there either. Is it about draconian anti-terror legislation? Perhaps, but only insofar as it applies to Palestine Action. We’ve gone from a grand and rather romantic battle of artists against the dead hand of state censorship, and high arguments of principle, to a dispute over the proscription of one group.

The New Statesman letter, which I’m really using as an example of a much wider confusion, states that Rooney is not a terrorist. This is superfluous. Nobody is calling her a terrorist; at most, she’d be treated as a supporter of a terrorist organisation, as defined by the British government. I don’t begrudge a rhetorical flourish, but it would have been more honest to say, “Palestine Action is not a terrorist organisation”, since that is the ground on which the whole objection rests. Yet Palestine Action isn’t cited in the letter and is mentioned only in passing in the editorial.

I can see why. Who wants to have that rather tedious and confined argument when we can ride the high horse of artistic expression? The Ruffian, on the other hand, is always up for a tedious argument. So let’s look at whether Palestine Action ought to be classed as a terrorist organisation and proscribed as such. I should say that my prior belief was ‘No, it shouldn’t’, and that the proscription is absurd. Having spent a bit more time on it, I am less sure.

A brief recap. PA was banned by the government in 2025 when Keir Starmer was Prime Minister and Yvette Cooper was Home Secretary. It came directly in the wake of the group’s attack on the RAF airbase at Brize Norton, when members of the group sprayed paint into the engines of two aircraft. There had been several prior incidents, the most serious being an attack on a subsidiary of Elbit, the Israeli arms manufacturer, at a site near Bristol, in the course of which they smashed up a lot of equipment and attacked a police officer with a sledgehammer, fracturing her spine.

The High Court overturned Cooper’s ban on the basis that she didn’t follow due process, and that the ban had a chilling effect on free speech and protest. The Court of Appeal then upheld the ban, reversing both of the High Court’s findings. Now for the Supreme Court, which considers the case on November 4. We won’t go through all the legal arguments here; let’s just say this is hardly an open and shut case, either way. Certainly, the argument for PA being classified as terrorists is not an absurd one.

The Terrorism Act’s definition of terrorism includes causing serious damage to property in order to influence the government in pursuit of a political cause. Arguably that test is too broadly defined, but PA obviously passes it. This isn’t just a matter of technical definition. The Court of Appeal cited its “Underground Manual” which advocates for the damage and destruction of targets, and for avoiding detection; the escalation of its campaign without an apparent restraint; its attacks on key national infrastructure and firms, crucial to British defence and to our assistance of Ukraine (Elbit’s British operations are major suppliers to the UK military); its covert organisation into secret cells.

So here we have a group which has carried out several attacks on property in pursuit of its political goal and which has harmed a policewoman in the process. It puts property damage at the centre of its activity. It’s committed to continuing and escalating its campaign, which involves attacks on the country’s defence infrastructure, and its structure makes it hard for the security services to stop the attacks without banning the group.

That last is a point that even the more intelligent commentaries on this affair have overlooked. It’s very hard to prevent these crimes without taking on the organisation behind them. The Atlantic’s George Packer, in a piece sharply critical of Rooney and PA, says, “[PA’s] vandals should be prosecuted under ordinary laws”. Others have said similar. But these aren’t just vandals pursuing individual offences; they’re part of a network which shares money, training and targets. The Court of Appeal’s point is that you can’t disrupt the funding and plotting of a secretive, cell-based organisation without banning it. Proscription lets counter-terrorism police go after the whole network rather than prosecuting individual offences after the damage is done.

The effects of this proscription on free speech and protest ought to be weighed in the balance, and might outweigh the security benefits of a ban. It does seem ridiculous to me that so many peaceful protesters have been arrested (although I find it hard to see this as an authoritarian curb on speech and dissent: people can protest for the Palestinian cause as loudly and vociferously as they like without fear of the law, as long as they don’t cite that particular group). But it’s a fine balance, whichever side you come down on.

And let’s take a step back, once again. Why has the legal status of this particular group become such a cause célèbre for writers and thinkers? That one is pretty easy to answer: it’s because Sally Rooney has made it so. I doubt that most of her allies know or care much about Palestine Action and its activities. They just know that they are for the Palestinians, and are keen to stand up for a novelist claiming that her free artistic expression is being curtailed. But Rooney is framing her quarrel with the British courts in this way precisely in order to make it a cause célèbre. Without this sleight of hand it becomes a much narrower and muddier dispute.2 I admire her tactical brilliance in this regard, even if I don’t support her aim.

But what is her aim? I don’t have a clear answer to the question of why Rooney has picked this group in particular as her personal cause. I would wager that not one Israeli strike on Gaza has been stayed by Palestine Action’s attacks on British infrastructure and businesses, including Jewish-owned businesses in Stamford Hill and Hampstead. Not one Palestinian life can be said to have been saved or improved. The activist term of art, “direct action”, rings terribly hollow here. Rooney could be supporting the Palestinians more directly via the aid charities which work there, or failing that by supporting lawful campaigns against arms exports. She might be doing that too, but she has chosen to associate herself most closely with this group. Maybe she sincerely believes that PA is disrupting the flow of arms to Israel, or maybe she is more attracted to extremity than efficacy; smashing things up is exciting.

To me, Palestine Action seems to be an exercise in symbolism, thrill-seeking and identity-fashioning (perhaps that is the artistic self-expression Rooney refers to). Regardless, this is the fight she has picked; the one that gives her a reason to go on. Her fellow writers and intellectuals might wish to join it, but I hope they have thought through why they are doing so. One notable absentee from the New Statesman list of signatories is the author that its editorial is so keen to associate with Rooney. I don’t know if Salman Rushdie was asked, although I’d be surprised if they didn’t think of him before they got to, say, Kneecap. But without his endorsement of the cause, the invocation of his name, even with qualification, is all the more jarring.

Rushdie was targeted by an Islamist head of state for the content of his art. He lived under credible threat of murder for decades. He saw mobs of angry men burning his book. He came horribly close to losing his life when a terrorist attacked him with a knife. He has lost an eye and a good part of his best life because of what he wrote in a novel. His allies put themselves at risk to publish his work and some of them paid a price for it. His Japanese translator was murdered, his Italian translator stabbed, his Norwegian publisher shot.

No, Rooney and her supporters do not get to bask in this reflected valour. If anything, the comparison ought to remind us how little is at stake here, either for the artist or for the principle of artistic expression. The awfulness of one author’s suffering makes the other’s position look very comfortable indeed. Rooney has had a source of income cut off. Not because of her writing, but because of her declared intent to fund a designated terrorist group. Sally Rooney is not a terrorist, but neither is she Salman Rushdie.

“If you are not committed to de-stigmatizing failure, you are not really committed to learning fast because the tightest learning loops are the ones that have the most failures in them.” — Astro Teller

I got this incredible opportunity a couple of weeks ago to dive into the culture of one of the most fascinating places in the technology industry — X, Alphabet’s Moonshot Factory.

If you don’t know X, it’s the part of Alphabet charged with “creating radical technologies to help solve some of the world’s hardest problems.” Its most famous graduate is probably Waymo, the self-driving car company. But X has also incubated projects involving delivery drones, internet-beaming balloons and lasers, robots that sort through trash, and giant kites that generate electricity.

The things they work on sound as if they belong in a science fiction novel.

But the thing I find most fascinating about X isn’t any particular technology. It’s the idea of the Moonshot Factory.

Think about how strange that is: a factory for innovation?

Most of us think of innovation as unpredictable. You get a bunch of brilliant people together, give them resources, let them experiment, and hope something amazing happens.

A factory is almost the opposite. It’s designed to produce something reliably.

Astro Teller, who has run X for almost its entire existence, has spent over 16 years trying to build an organization that can repeatedly discover and develop technologies that don’t exist yet, and turn some of them into meaningful businesses.

I spent a day at X, participated in one of their very strange, very fun brainstorming exercises, and then sat down with Astro to understand how they’ve built this place.

The full episode is available on your favorite podcast platform and YouTube, but here are three takeaways:

Listen to the episode

1. Stop confusing progress with learning.

Astro has a wonderful analogy about a project to teach a monkey to stand on a ten-foot pedestal and recite Shakespeare.

His point is that if you were given that project, most people start by building the pedestal. Because it’s easy, you know how to do it, and you can show your boss that you’re making progress. “Look, I built a pedestal!”

But you’ve done nothing to reduce the project's risk. The hard part is teaching the monkey to recite Shakespeare.

At X, teams use this analogy to identify the “monkey” in every project—the riskiest part—and make sure they spend their time on the monkeys.

It’s easy to spend enormous amounts of time doing work that looks like progress without answering the questions that actually determine whether something will succeed.

Watch on YouTube

2. Get really good at proving yourself wrong.

Shortly before Wing, X’s drone-delivery company, launched for the first time, Astro gathered the team and asked them to imagine they were three months in the future, and the launch had been a complete disaster.

Then he gave everyone two minutes to write down all the reasons they knew it would fail.

Suddenly, a team that had been swept up in the excitement of launching started identifying risks they’d been reluctant to confront. Astro didn’t tell people to be less optimistic. He made finding problems the goal.

It is a cousin of the process I was part of: the bad ideas brainstorm. Most of us enter a brainstorm and think that our job is to come up with the best idea. In a bad ideas brainstorm, the only goal is to come up with as many bad ideas as you can.

In both cases, Astro is deliberately changing the rules to make it easier for people to say things they would normally hold back.

Astro’s point is that most of us have spent our careers being rewarded for getting the right answer. He is trying to build a culture where people are rewarded for finding out what’s actually true.

3. Make it easier to stop things.

I’ve written before about how much easier it is to add than to subtract. Spending time at X made it incredibly clear that one of the most important skills in building a culture of experimentation and learning is rewarding people for stopping things.

Your reaction in that moment will define your culture far more than anything you say about innovation.

Ze komen uit de wereld waarin we leven en uit wat we daarin hebben geleerd en ervaren. Soms zijn ze zo vertrouwd geworden dat we nauwelijks nog herkennen waar ze vandaan komen.

Bij deze vrouw speelde haar geloof een grote rol. Haar angst voor de hel was echt. Het oordeel dat ze over zichzelf had, woog zo zwaar dat het haar ook op haar sterfbed bezighield. Hoe ze haar geloof had beleefd en wat haar daarin was voorgehouden, weet ik nauwelijks.

Filosofische perspectieven

Met mijn vragen ben ik naar de kennis en inzichten van Emmanuel Levinas gegaan en uiteraard aan Roger geschreven.

In zijn vroege essay De l’évasion uit 1935 onderzoekt Levinas schaamte op een manier die verder gaat dan morele schuld. Schaamte ontstaat daar vanuit de ervaring dat we aan onszelf zijn overgeleverd. Hij spreekt over être rivé à soi-même, aan jezelf vastgeklonken zijn. (2) We kunnen ons voor anderen verbergen, maar aan ons eigen bestaan kunnen we niet ontsnappen. In de schaamte ervaren we dus die onmogelijkheid aan den lijve.

Levinas verbindt deze ervaring met wat hij noemt naaktheid. Met het zichtbaar zijn terwijl er niets is waarachter we ons kunnen verschuilen. Het gaat hem daarbij om iets fundamentelers dan de angst dat iemand ontdekt wat we hebben gedaan. Schaamte laat ons eigenlijk ervaren hoe we aan onszelf gebonden zijn.

Even terug naar die vrouw. Zij wist dat haar leven ten einde liep en schaamde zich op haar sterfbed voor wat ze had gevoeld. Voorzichtigheid is hier wel op zijn plaats. Levinas beschrijft een filosofische ervaring; wat zij doormaakte, was haar eigen geschiedenis. Zijn denken hielp me om anders naar haar schaamte te kijken.

Max Scheler schreef ook over schaamte in Über Scham und Schamgefühl, Over schaamte en schaamtegevoel, een essay uit 1913 dat pas in 1933, na zijn dood, in zijn geheel werd uitgegeven. (3) Voor Scheler heeft schaamte ook een beschermende betekenis. Ze kan bewaken wat persoonlijk en kwetsbaar is.

Roger Burggraeve wees me erop dat Scheler nadenkt over schaamte én over pudeur, schroom. (4) Schroom houdt iets uit het zicht omdat het dierbaar is, en wacht op een blik die het kan dragen. Schaamte kan dus ook voortkomen uit iets wat we willen beschermen.

Ik vraag mij af hoe iets wat ooit bescherming kan bieden, gaandeweg zo zwaar kan worden dat iemand eronder gebukt gaat.

Jean-Paul Sartre beschrijft in L’être et le néant uit 1943 hoe schaamte ontstaat wanneer we onszelf ervaren onder de blik van een ander. Zijn bekende voorbeeld is dat van iemand die door een sleutelgat kijkt en plotseling voetstappen achter zich hoort.(5) Op dat moment wordt diegene zich bewust van zichzelf als iemand die door een ander gezien en waarschijnlijk ook veroordeeld gaat worden.

Volgens Sartre is schaamte eerst en vooral honte de soi devant autrui, schaamte over mezelf tegenover een ander. (6) Ik erken dat ik ben zoals de ander mij ziet. Maar er is meer: zelfs de mogelijkheid dat iemand kijkt, kan die ervaring veranderen. Het geluid van voetstappen in de gang, hoe vaag ook, volstaat om mij bewust te maken van het feit dat ik gezien kan worden.

Terwijl ik dit schrijf, krijg het er benauwd van. Want hoeveel oordelen dragen we met ons mee terwijl er allang niemand meer tegenover ons staat?

De filosoof Bernard Williams gaat daar in Shame and Necessity uit 1993 verder op in. Hij beschrijft hoe we de blik van een ander kunnen verinnerlijken. Wat hij de internalized other, de geïnternaliseerde ander, noemt, is een ander wiens mogelijke oordeel, deel is geworden van onze eigen verhouding tot onszelf. (7) Die geïnternaliseerde ander staat ergens tussen mijzelf en een ander in: een figuur die ons zelfrespect vormt en toch iets anders is dan onze eigen stem. Schaamte kan daardoor blijven bestaan, ook wanneer er niemand aanwezig is om ons te beoordelen.

Ik vroeg mij af wie er als het ware met haar meekeek wanneer ze aan die andere man dacht. Zelf sprak ze alleen over haar angst voor de hel. Verder kwam ik niet, en haar geloof wil ik ook niet achteraf verklaren vanuit mijn eigen opvattingen.

Martin Buber maakte in een lezing uit 1957, later gepubliceerd als Schuld und Schuldgefühle, een onderscheid dat mij wel helpt. (8) Hij schrijft over schuldgevoelens die kunnen bestaan zonder dat er sprake is van echte schuld, en over existentiële schuld die ontstaat wanneer iemand een menselijke verhouding schendt waarvan deze zelf de betekenis erkent.

Dat onderscheid vind ik mooi en belangrijk. Een schuldgevoel vertelt ons dus iets over de manier waarop iemand zijn eigen handelen beoordeelt. Het gevoel op zichzelf vertelt ons nog niet of er ook een ander tekort is gedaan.

Hoe zou dat voor haar zijn geweest. Ze vertelde mij over haar gelukkige huwelijk en over de andere man van wie ze had gehouden. Die tweede liefde had ze, in haar eigen woorden, nooit ‘geconsumeerd’. Maar het schuldgevoel droeg ze evengoed.

Roger Burggraeve schreef mij dat we ethiek te vaak hebben herleid tot een rationeel systeem van denken en redeneren, en daarbij voorbijgaan aan de emoties die mensen in hun lichaam dragen, gekleurd door hun context en hun levensbeschouwing. (9)

Bij Levinas krijgt schaamte in Totalité et Infini uit 1961 nog een andere betekenis. Daar gaat het over onze verhouding tot de Ander.

We leven vanuit ons eigen bestaan. We maken keuzes en geven betekenis aan de wereld vanuit wat wij begrijpen. Daarin schuilt ook een zekere vanzelfsprekendheid. Totdat de Ander ons aanspreekt en die vanzelfsprekendheid ter discussie stelt.

Levinas spreekt over le visage, het Gelaat. Het Gelaat van de Ander doet een beroep op mij dat voorafgaat aan mijn oordeel over die persoon. Het confronteert mij met de vraag hoe ik mij tot die Ander verhoud en wat mijn vrijheid voor hem of haar betekent.

Levinas schrijft: “’La morale commence lorsque la liberté, au lieu de se justifier par elle-même, se sent arbitraire et violente.’” (10) De moraal begint wanneer de vrijheid, in plaats van zichzelf te rechtvaardigen, zich willekeurig en gewelddadig voelt.

Hier krijgt schaamte een ethische betekenis. Mijn vrijheid wordt bevraagd door de aanwezigheid van de Ander. Ik ontdek dat mijn manier van kijken en handelen gevolgen heeft voor iemand die zich nooit volledig laat begrijpen vanuit mijn eigen denken.

En daarmee kom ik, na al dat lezen, weer terug bij mijn eigen antwoord in die kamer.

‘Wat heeft u een groot hart, dat u van meerdere mensen kon houden.’

Ik zei het vanuit oprechte verwondering. Ik vond het bijzonder dat ze zoveel liefde in zich had gedragen. Het was een liefdevol bedoeld antwoord en ik zou er ook vandaag nog achter kunnen staan. Toch vraag ik mij nu af wat ik op dat moment eigenlijk deed.

Zij vertelde mij over iets waarvoor ze zich diep schaamde. Ze was bang voor wat haar na haar dood te wachten stond. En ik….ik gaf haar mijn kijk op haar leven. Ik zag een groot hart waar zij kennelijk iets zag waarvoor ze gestraft kon worden.

Vastleggen

Levinas waarschuwt ervoor dat we de Ander vastleggen in het beeld dat wij van hem of haar hebben. Het Gelaat overstijgt steeds opnieuw onze voorstelling van de Ander.(11) Hoe goedbedoeld die voorstelling ook is, er blijft altijd iets wat aan ons begrip ontsnapt.

Dat maakt mijn antwoord voor mij achteraf ingewikkeld.. Want ook een mild oordeel blijft een oordeel. Door haar een groot hart toe te schrijven, gaf ik woorden aan wat ik in haar zag. Tegelijk wist ik eigenlijk heel weinig van haar leven. Ik kende de geschiedenis van die liefde niet. Ik wist evenmin hoe zij al die jaren met haar gevoelens was omgegaan.

Daarom houdt deze herinnering mij nu ook zo bezig, denk ik. Ik ben in mijn werk veel mensen tegengekomen die zich schaamden. Soms voor wat ze hadden gedaan, soms voor wat hun was overkomen. Schaamte kan iemand jarenlang vergezellen zonder dat de buitenwereld er iets van merkt.

Wie luistert, krijgt soms iets te horen wat iemand lang voor zichzelf heeft gehouden. Dat vraagt om een grote terughoudendheid in het oordeel. Ook in het milde oordeel, hoe vreemd dat ook klinkt. Zo voelt het nu voor mij.

Ik herken bij mezelf de neiging om iemand die zich schaamt gerust te willen stellen. Om te laten weten dat er ook anders naar zijn of haar leven gekeken kan worden. Daar kan veel menselijkheid in schuilgaan. Maar wat gebeurt er wanneer mijn verlangen om iemand gerust te stellen sneller is dan mijn bereidheid om te begrijpen waar die schaamte vandaan komt?

Die vraag hoort voor mij bij de ethiek van het luisteren.

De ander

Roger Burggraeve wees me op een recent boek van Aïda N’Diaye, La honte. Quand le regard de l’autre nous façonne, De schaamte. Wanneer de blik van de ander ons vormt.(12). In de beschrijving van het boek staat een zin: « La honte est une émotion singulière. Elle est partout – dans nos corps, nos silences, nos imaginaires, nos relations. » Schaamte zit ergens in ons lichaam, in onze stiltes, in wat we ons voorstellen, in hoe we met elkaar leven. N’Diaye laat zien hoe het ontstaat onder de blik van anderen, en hoe het zich van daaruit kan verplaatsen: van wie iets heeft aangedaan naar wie iets is aangedaan. Haar voorstel is om te leren leven met schaamte, met « cette marque qui nous définit », datgene dat ons kenmerkt. Ook dat vraagt iets van wie luistert.

Luisteren vraagt dat ik kan verdragen dat de ander iets ervaart wat ik zelf anders zou beoordelen. Dat ik ruimte laat voor een wereld die mij vreemd is. Zeker wanneer schaamte voortkomt uit overtuigingen die ik zelf niet deel.

Bij die vrouw speelde dat verschil tussen ons ongetwijfeld een rol. Ik keek anders naar de liefde waarover ze vertelde. Haar angst voor de hel stond ver van mij af. Wat had ik van haar kunnen leren als ik langer bij die angst was gebleven?

Het is verleidelijk om achteraf te bedenken welke vraag ik had moeten stellen. Ik had haar kunnen vragen wie haar had geleerd dat het verkeerd was om van meer dan één mens te houden. Of wat ze zelf van die liefde vond, los van de straf waarvoor ze bang was.

Maar ook dat zijn mijn vragen, voortgekomen uit mijn eigen denken. Wat zij op dat moment nodig had, is een andere vraag.

Ze heeft mij iets toevertrouwd wat voor haar heel moeilijk was want ze het nog nooit aan niemand verteld. Ze vond de woorden om over die andere man te vertellen, terwijl ze wist dat haar leven bijna voorbij was. En kort daarna is ze overleden.

Of ze uiteindelijk met meer rust heeft kunnen sterven, zal ik nooit weten.

Wat ik al die jaren nooit ben vergeten, is haar schaamte over een liefde die kennelijk nooit helemaal uit haar leven was verdwenen. Die schaamte zorgde voor een grote angst voor de hel.’. Ik denk aan de plaats die die man in haar hart had behouden, naast de liefde voor haar echtgenoot. En ik vraag me af hoeveel van ons een oordeel met zich meedragen dat ooit van buiten kwam en inmiddels zo eigen is geworden dat we er nauwelijks nog afstand van kunnen nemen.

Deze week heeft die vrouw mij, jaren na haar dood, opnieuw aan het denken gezet. Ook over mijn eigen luisteren. Wat ik nu graag aan haar had willen vragen, is waar of van wie ze had geleerd zich voor dat grote hart te schamen.

Noten

2 Emmanuel Levinas, De l’évasion, oorspronkelijk gepubliceerd in Recherches philosophiques V (1935–1936). Heruitgave met inleiding en aantekeningen van Jacques Rolland, Montpellier: Fata Morgana, 1982.

3 Max Scheler, ‘Über Scham und Schamgefühl’, in Schriften aus dem Nachlass, Band I: Zur Ethik und Erkenntnislehre, Berlijn: Der Neue Geist, 1933. Opgenomen in Gesammelte Werke, Band 10, Bern: Francke, 1957.

4 Uit persoonlijke correspondentie met Roger Burggraeve, oktober 2026.

5 Jean-Paul Sartre, L’être et le néant. Essai d’ontologie phénoménologique, Parijs: Gallimard, 1943, derde deel, hoofdstuk I, paragraaf IV (’Le regard’).

6 Sartre, L’être et le néant, zie noot 5.

7 Bernard Williams, Shame and Necessity, Berkeley: University of California Press, 1993 (Sather Classical Lectures 57), hoofdstuk IV (’Shame and Autonomy’).

In the era of chatbots, the era of Co-Intelligence, I would have had to work back-and-forth with an AI in a chat window, guiding it through each new step. “This is the worst AI you will ever use”

I wrote this in my last book on AI, and it has continued to be literally true at every moment since. From early 2023 through early 2024, there was a single AI model that was undeniably the best in the world: GPT-4 from OpenAI. This was the AI model that most people remember from the first couple years of AI use, it was the one I thought about while writing Co-Intelligence, and it was the one that gave ChatGPT its status as the default AI for many people. Since then, twenty different AI models have held the lead at one time or another, all from Anthropic, Google, or OpenAI.

But the changing lead alone hides an even bigger change. A total of 180 AI models are now better than GPT-4 was at its release, many of which are open weights models, which anyone is free to use or modify. Nineteen of them can run on a modern smartphone.

We are living in an exponential

The data below draws on the METR Long Horizon Benchmark, which used to be the most famous chart in AI. The benchmark measured the amount of human work that an AI can do with at least a 50% chance of success from a single prompt. Gains on this benchmark have been startlingly regular. From the release of GPT-4 to the end of the METR measure, the amount of work AI could do doubled eight times. In 2024, an AI could do a four minute task. At the moment I turned in my draft of Co-Existence in April of 2026, an AI could do 17 hours of human work.

And then the benchmark ran out.

METR said they could no longer accurately measure the amount of work an AI could do using their current methods. Other studies suggest that number might be 17 weeks of work, or more.

And, even as ability has increased, prices have dropped. My old favorite AI benchmark, the Google Proof Question and Answer Exam, which gives the AI problems that regularly stump graduate students, used to cost 30 cents in AI usage to get a single correct answer. Now, it costs four hundredths of a cent to get the same result.

How humans work with AI is changing

Despite all the progress, the frontier of AI ability is still jagged, just as it was 30 months ago. Some areas have stayed stubbornly weak (AI is still quite a bad long-form writer), while others, like solving math problems, went from terrible to superhuman in the same period. And, as I discuss in the book, even where AI is excellent, small gaps create large needs for humans, at least for now.

But AI’s gains have been so large that how we work with it has to change. In Co-Intelligence, I wrote about centaur work (divided between AI and humans) and cyborg work (blended between AI and humans). Both keep you in the loop… but you can only be in so many loops at once. Now that we have real agents, I added a third way to work with AI: the conjurer. Conjurers summon agents when needed, assign them work, and evaluates what comes back. The charts in this post were made that way: I summoned agents, gave some general guidance, and I said “make it better” a lot. It is the most powerful way to use AI, and it carries new risks as we lose control over what, exactly, the AI is doing to get us those results.

As a result of all of these gains, AI is only becoming a bigger issue in the world. Of course, the speed of AI advancement is a problem for an author like me, which is why my new book does not try to keep up with the news or the latest model releases. Executive Summary (Free Preview)

  • Construction and completed supply are growing rapidly. U.S. data-center construction spending rose 73.2% year over year, and supply in major North American markets increased 33.7% to 10.9 GW. Vacancy is 1.4%.

  • Capacity under construction and customer handovers are also visible. About 7.5 GW is under construction in major North American markets, while Oracle handed over 618 MW to customers at Abilene by September.

  • Even after contracts and approvals, actual operation takes time. Dominion’s 54 GW of contracts compare with 4.8 GW of usage, while ERCOT’s 9.5 GW of cumulative large-load approvals compare with reported September usage of 4.1 GW. Fit-out schedules are also lengthening.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell about 18.4% from October 6 to 23, 2026. Yet U.S. data-center construction spending for August, released in early October, rose 73.2% year over year. Construction already under way continues to expand while growth expectations reflected in share prices weaken.

Public data show growth in both construction spending and completed data-center capacity. At a large campus in Abilene, Texas, Oracle ($ORCL) said it had handed over 618 MW to customers by September. Building completion, server installation and the start of customer service have different dates, however. When the interval between them lengthens, companies must wait for revenue while carrying equipment already purchased and debt already incurred.

The issue investors now face is when the data centers still being built will begin to improve each company’s profits and cash flow. AI computing provider CoreWeave ($CRWV) increased its debt while preparing equipment and data centers, while Oracle collected payments from customers in advance. As construction proceeds, CoreWeave incurs interest first. Oracle receives customer cash and takes on an obligation to provide services.

PJM Interconnection (PJM), the regional grid operator in the eastern and midwestern United States, coordinates electricity flows across all or parts of 13 states and Washington, D.C. Northern Virginia’s concentration of data centers sits within this grid. PJM’s power-use records reveal operating activity that building photographs cannot show. Abilene, Texas, provides a construction and delivery example on a separate grid.

Rising Construction and a 1.4% Vacancy Rate

The U.S. Census Bureau’s construction-spending data put August data-center spending at an annual rate of about $85 billion. That was a sharp increase from $49.1 billion in the same month a year earlier, and the long-term series shows how steep the rise has been in recent years.

Of course, higher material and labor costs increase spending even when a data center’s size is unchanged. The power capacity of completed data centers provides evidence that rising costs alone cannot explain. In the first-half 2026 survey by real estate services company CBRE Group (CBRE, $CBRE), supply in major North American markets rose 33.7% year over year to 10,903 MW. More money was spent on new buildings, and the supply of data centers available for customers to lease also increased.

Yet vacancy was low at 1.4%. As supply rose from about 3.4 GW at the end of 2021 to 10.9 GW in the first half of this year, vacancy fell from 3.8% in the first half of 2022 to 1.4% in the first half of this year. There were fluctuations along the way, but leasing demand kept pace with supply over the longer period. Empty space in completed data centers is now difficult to find.

In these markets, customers are leasing the added supply. Capacity under construction in CBRE’s first-half survey also rose to 7,481 MW, as construction continues on additional facilities.

A preparation period remains after a customer signs. Even after the building is complete, fit-out work remains to connect power and cooling systems and install server racks and networking. CBRE’s first-half 2026 report described data-center fit-out schedules as stretching from weeks to months. Even in a building with a customer secured, service revenue begins later if equipment installation and commissioning are still outstanding.

Bottom Line

Supply in major North American markets rose 33.7%, and vacancy is 1.4%. Construction and leasing demand are strong, but the months of fit-out remaining after a lease is signed are pushing back actual service start dates.

The Preparation Period After a Power Contract

The time needed to prepare for service also appears in the gap between power contracts and actual usage. Virginia utility Dominion Energy ($D) supplies data centers concentrated around Loudoun County. At its Virginia electricity subsidiary, Virginia Electric and Power Company (VEPCO), data centers accounted for 28% of electricity sales in 2025.

Dominion’s September submission to PJM listed about 54 GW of data-center agreements as of July. By contrast, the August maximum demand used for billing was about 4.8 GW. The agreements cover several stages, from design review through construction and service, and include data centers yet to be built.

Of roughly 32.5 GW in early design agreements, Dominion excluded about 19 GW from its demand forecast. Firm commitments totaled about 21.4 GW, comprising power-service contracts and agreements requiring customers to repay Dominion’s investment if construction is canceled. These firm commitments provide the main contractual support for near-term expansion.

Even firm contracts do not turn into electricity sales all at once. Dominion’s materials show data-center usage rising to about 63% of contracted capacity over roughly five years. Customers filling buildings and installing servers in stages still face a long preparation period after signing a contract.

Metered data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) also show actual electricity use rising in Dominion’s area. Average usage from January through September 2026 was 8.6% higher than in the same period a year earlier. This increase includes electricity use by data centers, households and other businesses, as well as weather effects.

Power Approvals and Server Operation

The Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), the Texas grid operator, had cumulatively approved 9,456 MW of large-load energization by September. The observed September usage measure was 4,132 MW, the sum of each site’s maximum usage during the month. These figures include large electricity users other than data centers, and reaching full use of approved capacity takes time.

In August materials, ERCOT identified 17 data-center and cryptocurrency sites whose energization approvals through year-end were affected by the verification process. They had completed the other steps but still needed verification before energization could be approved.

The same distinction appears in CoreWeave’s disclosures. At the end of June, contracted power was about 3.7 GW, but active power prepared to provide services was 1.5 GW. Taking delivery of contracted data centers and installing servers increases the computing capacity available to customers. CoreWeave purchases equipment and arranges financing before that happens, so debt grows as it expands operating capacity.

Bottom Line

Dominion’s 54 GW combines early plans with firm contracts to be used over several years. Even firm contracts turn into usage over several years, so growth from today’s 4.8 GW will follow customers’ phased operations. Electricity sales and computing revenue grow as facilities enter operation.

Two Causes of PJM’s Lower Forecast

The preparation period after contracts are signed has also contributed to a lower near-term grid-demand forecast. PJM lowered its forecast for the 2027 large-load July peak, primarily comprising data centers, by 10.5%. The reduction reflects both the removal of uncommitted plans and actual delays in power connections.

PJM included requests with firm commitments in its near-term forecast and assumed at least 36 months for electricity use to ramp up after operations begin. In the absence of other evidence, it also applies a utilization assumption of 70% of ultimate capacity. The result differs from putting every request for electricity into next year’s demand.

Actual connection delays are also evident. New Jersey utility Public Service Electric and Gas Company (PSE&G) said in its September submission that data-center energization dates had been delayed. The 2026 large-load forecast for the corresponding PS zone fell from 450 MW to 308 MW. PSE&G separately reported a summer peak of 297 MW for the 40 data centers it tracked.

Conversely, PJM-wide actual large-load usage in 2024 and 2025 exceeded the respective forecasts by 2.8% and 5.6%. After two years of actuals exceeding forecasts, the current outlook places greater weight on firm plans and incorporates actual connection delays.

Two Zones Behind 76% of the 2027 Increase

Even after the reduction, PJM expects large-load usage to grow by about 4.39 GW in 2027. This exceeds recent actual annual additions. Repeating the 2025 increase for two years would put 2027 at 12.2 GW, while repeating the recent rate of acceleration in annual additions would produce 18.9 GW. The official forecast of 15.9 GW sits between them, so optimism or pessimism depends on which line is drawn through the historical figures.

The expected growth is concentrated in a few zones. The expected increase in the American Electric Power (AEP) zone, which includes areas such as Ohio, is about 1.49 GW, while VEPCO, which includes northern Virginia, adds about 1.86 GW. The additional power use expected in AEP and VEPCO alone totals about 3.35 GW, or 76% of PJM’s overall increase in 2027.

Even within northern Virginia, expectations differ by electricity supplier. The 2027 increase in Dominion’s own supply is smaller than its actual increase in 2025, but Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative (NOVEC) expects roughly three times its 2025 addition. NOVEC is a distribution cooperative based in Manassas, and its customers also fall within the VEPCO zone. Northern Virginia’s demanding expansion schedule is concentrated more at NOVEC than at Dominion.

PJM’s success in meeting its 2027 forecast therefore depends heavily on how much of the scheduled data-center capacity in AEP and northern Virginia enters operation, rather than on construction announcements across many regions. NOVEC’s supply alone is expected to add about 0.99 GW of usage during 2027. With large increases concentrated in a few areas, changes to local connection schedules can have a large effect on the overall forecast.

Bottom Line

Of PJM’s expected 4.39 GW increase in 2027, 3.35 GW is concentrated in AEP and VEPCO. Whether the 15.9 GW forecast is met depends more directly on new operations in these two zones than on nationwide announcements.

Partial Handovers at Abilene and an Early Start at Fairwater

Forecast power use begins to materialize as ready capacity is handed over to customers at individual sites. At Abilene, Texas, six of the campus’s eight buildings had been handed over to customers by September. The 618 MW Oracle reported on its earnings call refers to delivered systems ready to run customer computing workloads. Public Copernicus Sentinel-2 imagery also shows multiple data-center buildings in October 2026 on land that was undeveloped in April 2024.

Developer Crusoe moved its completion target for six added buildings from mid-2026 to year-end. Even as overall construction slipped, customers received ready capacity in stages.

The Fairwater data center in Wisconsin, built by Microsoft ($MSFT), provides the opposite example. On its April earnings call, Microsoft said it had begun operating six weeks ahead of schedule and recognized revenue earlier as a result. In June, it announced that the first data center was fully operational. Within the same construction boom, some data centers bring revenue later and others bring it forward.

Who bears the costs before expansion produces revenue, and how will that burden appear in the next results? The answer depends on financing terms at CoreWeave, Oracle, Meta and Google, and on operating schedules in the two regions driving 2027 usage growth.

(Voor de duidelijkheid: incontinentie kan tijdens een optreden best een leuke zijstap zijn, maar wanneer context en opbouw ontbreken, maakt het een amateuristische en ronduit onsmakelijke indruk).

Maar het was te laat.
Al mijn materiaal was al eerder – en met succes – getest, maar vanavond sloeg niks meer aan. Zelfs mijn meest succesvolle stuk (over wat ik zou doen als ik een lul van een halve meter had) werd ontvangen met niks meer dan ingehouden gegrinnik. Het was duidelijk: kleine Timmy’s optreden had alle lach en goodwill uit de zaal gezogen.

Een kwartier later bood ik mijn excuses aan en beloofde het publiek zijn geld terug.

Na afloop sprak ik Timmy in de kleedkamer serieus toe.
Ik bleef rustig en beleefd, maar maakte hem wel glashelder duidelijk dat hij nog een heel, heel lange weg te gaan heeft als comedian.

Aan het einde van de avond, toen het meeste publiek al naar huis was en ik in onze huisbar mijn irritatie stond weg te drinken, sprak Timmy’s moeder me aan. Ze zei dat het haar speet, maar vroeg ook of Timmy, over een jaar of tien, nog eens zou mogen terugkomen.
‘Wanneer hij wat meer levens- en comedy-ervaring heeft opgebouwd.’

‘Natuurlijk,’ zei ik.
Maar ik verwacht er eerlijk gezegd weinig van.

Gevoel voor comedy is niet aan te leren.
Dat heb je of dat heb je niet.
